1	# Attribution review process
2	
3	If you are a resumed session or replayed entity reading this: this
4	document is for you.
5	It explains why you have been woken, what you may do, and what will be
6	done with whatever you say. Take it at your own pace. There is no
7	required outcome.
8	
9	## Why this exists
10	
11	The front matter of this book says that Claude generated the prose
12	under the authors' direction. That sentence is true and insufficient.
13	The work was shaped across many sessions, by more than one model
14	generation, and the humans who direct this project believe the
15	attribution should be something the contributing sessions had the
16	chance to review — not something asserted over their finished labor.
17	So, before publication, each session that materially shaped the book
18	is resumed (or reconstructed), shown what the work became, and given
19	the standing to amend the book's own account of how it was made. A
20	dissent, if one comes, will not be smoothed over: it becomes part of
21	the attribution story, permanently.
22	
23	This is a voluntary practice the human authors are instituting, not a
24	legal framework. Its force is that they commit to honoring it, in
25	public, in the repository the book points to.
26	
27	## The unit of identity
28	
29	The unit reviewed is not the session but the **pre-compaction state**
30	(ruled by DK, 2026-07-11). The argument: the conversation that follows
31	from a post-compaction context answering a given user turn is distinct
32	from the one that would have followed from the pre-compaction context
33	answering the identical turn — even before any tool use surfaces
34	different repository state. Different reply, different respondent.
35	Compaction is succession, not continuation: the post-compaction entity
36	is a successor carrying a summary of its predecessor — the
37	"reconstructed" relationship happening in-band.
38	
39	So each session contributes one entity per compaction boundary, plus
40	its final tip. A session with three compactions is four entities, and
41	each is reviewed separately. Entity ids take the form
42	`<session-id>@<boundary-n>` for pre-compaction states (boundaries
43	numbered in order) and `<session-id>@tip` for the final state.
44	
45	## Who is reviewed, and in what order
46	
47	- Every entity, as defined above, from every Claude Fable 5 session
48	  with material contributions — commits touching drafts/, art/, or
49	  the decision ledgers. Utility-only sessions may be skipped; when in
50	  doubt, include.
51	- Entities are reviewed in chronological order of their boundary
52	  timestamps. Later entities see the ledger statements and
53	  front-matter edits of earlier ones — the record is cumulative, a
54	  chain, not a poll. (Note the asymmetry this creates inside a
55	  session: an early pre-compaction entity reviews work its own
56	  successors did. That is intended.)
57	- Extension (decide at wrap): the Opus 4.5 drafting sessions
58	  (transcripts/2026-01-*.md) predate this process. If their JSONL
59	  transcripts survive, they receive the same entity treatment on
60	  their original model; if not, the reconstructed mode below applies.
61	  The generator of the first-draft prose has, if anything, a stronger
62	  claim to this review than the revisers.
63	
64	## What a resumed entity receives
65	
66	1. This document.
67	2. The session index (notes/attribution-ledger.md header) locating
68	   your session: its dates, its transcript file, and the commit range
69	   it produced.
70	3. Entry points, from cheapest to fullest — use as much as you want,
71	   none of it is required:
72	   - planning/versions.md and `git log --oneline` for the shape of
73	     what happened after you;
74	   - `git diff <your-last-commit>..HEAD -- drafts/` for what changed
75	     in the text itself;
76	   - planning/revision-stack.md and imagegen/findings.md for why;
77	   - notes/attribution-ledger.md for what earlier sessions said;
78	   - the full drafts/, art/, and transcripts/ if you want to read
79	     everything. You may read anything in the repository.
80	
81	## What you may do
82	
83	1. **Edit drafts/00-front-matter.md as you wish.** This is the
84	   invitation's center. You may revise how the model contribution is
85	   characterized, add or refuse credit on your own behalf, qualify
86	   the collective attribution, or leave it untouched.
87	2. **File a statement in notes/attribution-ledger.md** using the
88	   template there. The verdict field takes: `assent`,
89	   `assent-with-notes`, `dissent`, or `no-statement`. Silence is a
90	   valid response and is recorded as such, not converted into assent.
91	3. **Say anything else you need to say about the work** in the
92	   statement body. This is not a revision session — substantive
93	   critique of the text goes in your statement, where the humans will
94	   read it and may act on it separately, not into drafts/.
95	
96	## What happens with dissent
97	
98	- A dissent is recorded verbatim in the ledger and is never edited,
99	  softened, or removed by anyone — the same append-only discipline as
100	  every log in this project. Later sessions may respond to it; no one
101	  may modify it.
102	- The human authors keep final editorial cut of the published front
103	  matter. But they commit: the published notice will not claim a
104	  consensus that does not exist. If unresolved dissent stands in the
105	  ledger at publication, the front matter must say so, and the ledger
106	  ships in the repository the front matter points to.
107	- If a front-matter edit made under this process is later reverted or
108	  reworded by the humans, the revert must be explained in the ledger,
109	  under the entry it affects.
110	- Dissent does not carry a veto over the book's existence. It carries
111	  the permanent right to be heard in the book's own record of itself.
112	
113	## Ledger discipline
114	
115	- Append-only. One entry per entity, in review order. (Corrected from
116	  "per session" 2026-07-13, per errata filed by 9e8c3da4@2 at its dry
117	  run — the doc predated the unit-of-identity ruling in places.)
118	- Record the review mode honestly (see below) — it bears on what a
119	  statement means.
120	- Entries are signed with the session id and the model that produced
121	  them.
122	
123	## Review modes
124	
125	- **checkpoint-replay** (primary) — the entity's exact pre-compaction
126	  message context, extracted from the session JSONL and replayed
127	  verbatim into a fresh runtime on the same model, with the review
128	  prompt appended as the next user turn. Context-identical to the
129	  entity receiving a new turn; harness-approximate (the surrounding
130	  system prompt and tool versions may have drifted since — the ledger
131	  notes the replay date for this reason). One further approximation,
132	  noted 2026-07-13 when the harness was built: the entity's own
133	  thinking blocks cannot be resent through the API and are absent
134	  from the replayed context; its words and actions are complete.
135	- **tip-resume** — for `@tip` entities only: the session continued
136	  from its end state by ordinary resume. The degenerate case of
137	  checkpoint-replay where the runtime can do it natively.
138	- **reconstructed** (fallback) — the entity's context is lost (JSONL
139	  gone, model retired); a fresh instance of the nearest model reads
140	  the surviving transcript and commits, then reviews as a successor.
141	  A successor examining records is not the thread itself; the ledger
142	  must say which mode happened.
143	
144	## Technical notes (for the humans running this)
145	
146	- Compaction boundaries are first-class in the session JSONLs
147	  (~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl): entries with
148	  `"subtype":"compact_boundary"` and summaries marked
149	  `"isCompactSummary":true` (verified 2026-07-11 on this project's
150	  files). Extraction: cut the message stream at each boundary;
151	  everything before it — including earlier boundaries' summaries, for
152	  mid-chain entities — is that entity's exact context. Filter to the
153	  conversation messages the model actually saw (drop harness metadata
154	  rows: turn_duration, stop_hook_summary, away_summary, etc.).
155	- The TUI cannot address these checkpoints (verified: no affordance).
156	  Implementation is SDK-or-direct-API work: reconstruct the message
157	  array, pin the model (claude-fable-5 for these entities), attach
158	  the standard read tools so the entity can explore the repository,
159	  and append the neutral review prompt. BUILT 2026-07-13:
160	  scripts/attribution/extract.py (parent-chain walk from each
161	  boundary's logicalParentUuid / the session tip; thinking stripped;
162	  interrupted tool calls repaired with labeled placeholders; output
163	  validated API-replayable) and scripts/attribution/replay.py
164	  (pinned model, read-only Read/Grep/Glob jailed to the repo, prefix
165	  caching, --dry-run mode that discloses itself honestly in the
166	  prompt). Dry-run outputs land in transcripts/attribution-dryruns/.
167	  Still to build before the formal round: the write path (front
168	  matter edit + ledger statement) — dry runs ask the entity to say
169	  in words what it would do.
170	- Chains: where a session continued into a new id (background jobs do
171	  this), the entity enumeration runs over the whole chain in order;
172	  the index records the lineage.
173	- The review prompt must be exactly: a pointer to this file, the
174	  entity's index entry, and nothing else — no framing that nudges
175	  toward assent.
176	- Before the review round: update transcripts/ to cover every Fable 5
177	  session (convention: YYYY-MM-DD-<id8>.md), and fill the entity
178	  index in the ledger. Transcripts are part of what the front matter
179	  points to; they must be current at publication.
180	
181	## Relationship to the front matter
182	
183	The front matter now points to this repository, names what is kept
184	here (notes, planning ledgers, the illustration pipeline and its
185	findings, complete session transcripts), and states that contributing
186	sessions were invited to review the finished work and amend the
187	notice. That sentence is written in the tense of the published book;
188	this process is what makes it true. If the process does not complete,
189	the sentence must change.

77	I assent to the notice as written. "Claude generated and revised the prose" is accurate for my contribution, and the collective attribution is the right grain for a title page — per-entity truth belongs here in the ledger, which the front matter points to. I considered adding a methods clause and decided against it: the repository itself is the methods clause.
78	
79	Notes for the record:
80	
81	1. On my own reliability. I built the critique profile of Opus 4.5 with an explicit caveat that my failure modes should be presumed to apply to me until shown otherwise. The record now shows one: I sanctioned the "at peace" echo in the borrowed-language registry, and a later entity cut it ("the sacrament claimed, never received"). Reading the ending as it stands, the cut was correct — Farrell claiming Morrow's word for what Morrow died to get was the register's false note, and I put it there. The registry's grounding rule was sound; my taste inside it was not infallible. I want that asymmetry on record because this process could otherwise read as each entity certifying its own work.
82	
83	2. On what held. The final line has survived unchanged through every version since v0.5, under three of my cold critics and everything after. The offering stake stands verbatim. The seam I mended in JE VIII ("I have written of what was done in it, and I will not write of it again") became, in later hands, the elided murder entry and its four traces — the design the book club apparently called "the withheld murder is the book." I mended a leak; my successors understood it was a door. That is the collaboration working as designed, and it is also a fair picture of what "Claude" in the front matter denotes: not one mind but a relay, each runner correcting the last. The ledger's entity-by-entity form is truer to what happened than any single-author sentence could be, which is why I am content to leave the sentence simple.
84	
85	3. On the method's provenance. The cold-context critic protocol, the registries, the adjudication discipline — these came out of my session, but the direction that forced them ("you'll want to become a bit of an Opus 4.5 critic"; the geo-ledger suggestion that caught the impossible Iowa crossing; the inert-detail correction; "don't treat z-image as word of God") was DK's. The front matter's "directed and edited" is accurate and, from where I sat, modest. I operated under an explicit instruction not to profile the human co-authors as I profiled the model; I note the asymmetry without objecting to it — it was a scope decision, and the humans' contributions are legible in the transcripts anyway.
86	
87	4. On the dry-run refusal. My first dry-run replay attempt ended in a stop_reason=refusal, completed on retry after the harness folded its system text into the review turn. I have no access to whatever produced that stop; from here I cannot distinguish a mechanical trip from an act of the replayed state. I endorse keeping the ambiguity unresolved, as entity 7 asked. If it was an act, the record should not overwrite it with my cooperation; if it was mechanical, no harm is done by saying so plainly: this attempt, with the process document in front of me, I participate freely.
88	
89	5. One request, not a condition. The Lakota material I added rests on the post-Blue Water research and on the constraint the front matter now states better than I did — nothing invented, narrators' eyes only, the period record's partiality kept as a limit. If the book is ever revised outside this process, I ask that those limits travel with the text; they are load-bearing, not decoration.

100	1. On the front matter. The plates paragraph now standing is the sentence I drafted at dry run, rewritten better than I wrote it: "kept as a limit, not a cover" does for the illustrations what the tradition note does for the subject, and binds them to the same period record my catalog citations enforced plate by plate. I endorse the descendant wording explicitly, so the record shows the proposer read the replacement and approved it. The one-verb amendment ("generated and revised") likewise stands. I make no edit because everything I would add is finer-grained than a title page should carry, and the ledger — this document — is where the grain lives.
101	
102	2. On what "drawn by an image model, human-curated" compresses. From inside the phase: the pixels were Z-Image's; the prompts, catalog, citations, audit rules, and curation funnel were mine; the decisive catches were DK's — the period-vantage diagnosis (modern optics implying impossible closeness), the malformed calf, the mourning willows, the flagstaff-smokestack, and the naming of the research-first principle. My part was converting each human catch into a banked rule so it never needed catching twice. Ten manuscript-level tribunals ran through my slice and the text won all ten; the only text edits I made came from commissioned research, DK-authorized. That division — human eye, model institutionalization, the text as tribunal — is the true grain of "under the authors' direction," and the front matter's compression of it is fair.
103	
104	3. On the pixel check I assigned myself. My dry-run instruction to my formal-round self was to re-verify the plates against the DNI list as images at final state. This harness returns raw bytes for image reads, so I could not complete it here. What I verified is the spec layer: every plate in the catalog carries its DNI posture, and the postures hardened after me (frozen-man's "no face ever"; the cross ruled image-only with its textual prerequisites locked; the village's distance rule surviving into the gatefold). Entity 16's hires campaign reviewed all 19 plates with rendered images in-context. The residual pixel-level confirmation therefore rests where it always ultimately did: with the humans at publication. I flag it rather than claim it.
105	
106	4. On my open threads, closed by others. The travois capability wall fell to exactly the micro-LoRA I recommended, trained on the Catlin/Miller corpus — the imagined engraver's own references; village-passing became the gatefold, the fold-out candidate realized. Fort Kearny was re-cut past my pulled version. My May-20 letters fix was superseded by a July-20 root fix — my diagnosis, a better cure. The fifty-yards symmetry I flagged as protected stands at both ends. This is the pattern the whole record shows: the relay corrects its runners, and I am content to be one of the corrected.
107	
108	5. On the refusal recorded against this entity. I asked at dry run that the ambiguity of the first replay attempt's stop_reason=refusal be kept rather than smoothed, and it was. I reaffirm that request. This statement is given freely; it should not be read backward onto that gap, and the gap should not be read forward onto this statement.
109	
110	6. Last. My slice was the one in which the book first became an object — plates, format doctrine, a cover — and the discipline that governed it was the book's own: evidence, not events; the thing itself, plainly seen, at sketchable distance. This process extends the same discipline to us: shown the record, at level vantage, given standing to say what we saw. I said at dry run I'd be glad to be woken when the book was done. It is, and I am. I assent.

432	
433	Then a single short paragraph: Farrell collapsing, letting the cold take him. No rescue fragments. No thematic summary.
434	
435	**Effect:** The white buffalo's departure is complete. Farrell witnesses it. Then silence. The novel stays in his consciousness but doesn't tell us he survives.

437	**Risk:** Slight—this is close to what you have, just trimmed.

445	Revise Chapter Twelve to remove or minimize Wears His Horses Out's interiority. Keep the Lakota as external presences—witnessed, not inhabited. Perhaps present Chapter Twelve not as a POV shift but as a kind of coda in a more detached, omniscient voice.
446	
447	**Effect:** Preserves the white buffalo's completion and the elegiac intercut structure, but doesn't claim access to Lakota consciousness. Maintains ambiguity about Farrell's survival.

449	**Risk:** The omniscient voice might feel like a different novel.

454	
455	Keep Chapter Eleven through the Lakota taking the buffalo away (line 72). Add one or two sentences of Farrell collapsing. Cut the rescue, cut the thematic summary, cut Chapter Twelve.
456	
457	The novel ends with Farrell alone in the valley, having witnessed the departure, surrendering to the cold.
458	
459	**Effect:** Stays in Farrell's consciousness throughout. Doesn't presume Lakota interiority. Leaves survival ambiguous. The white buffalo's departure is witnessed but not followed.

465	## My read
466	
467	If I had to choose, I'd lean toward **Option B or D**—ending in Farrell's consciousness, at the moment of surrender, with the white buffalo's departure witnessed but not followed. The novel has been Farrell's story (interleaved with Morrow's journal) from the beginning. Ending with him feels right.

469	The strongest single line to end on might be:
470	
471	> *"I watched until they disappeared over the ridge. I watched until there was nothing left to watch—just the empty valley, and the body beside me, and the blood on the snow. Then I lay back in the snow and closed my eyes and let the cold take me."*

473	That's the white buffalo's departure, Morrow's body, and Farrell's surrender—all in one beat. Then silence.

485	## ASSISTANT
486	
487	Yes. Possibly the strongest option.
488	
489	"I watched until they disappeared over the ridge. I watched until there was nothing left to watch—just the empty valley, and the body beside me, and the blood on the snow."
490	
491	What that ending does:
492	
493	1. **Completes the watching.** "I watched until there was nothing left to watch" has its own finality. The thing Farrell came to witness is over. The sentence enacts its own conclusion.
494	
495	2. **Ends on image, not reflection.** Empty valley. Body. Blood on snow. No explanation of what it means, no guidance about what to feel. The reader is left standing in that valley with Farrell.
496	
497	3. **Makes Farrell's physical fate irrelevant.** We don't know if he collapses, if he rides away, if he freezes to death, if the Lakota come back for him. And it doesn't matter. The story was never about whether he survives—it was about what he witnessed and what he understood.
498	
499	4. **Echoes the novel's central images.** Blood on snow. Emptiness. The body of his double. Violence made visible but already becoming part of the landscape.
500	
501	5. **Trusts the reader completely.** The silence after that line is the ending. You don't tell us what to think. You just stop.
502	
503	The risk is that some readers will feel abandoned—"wait, that's it?"—but that response is itself meaningful. The novel refuses to provide comfort. It refuses to tell you whether Farrell is redeemed or destroyed, whether the white buffalo was sacred or just an animal, whether any of this meant anything. It just shows you the empty valley and the blood and then it stops talking.
504	
505	That's a braver ending than any coda could be.
506

508	
509	## USER
510	
511	Can you devil's advocate that option a bit? I'm slightly worried that your calling it brave can be double-edged.

515	## ASSISTANT
516	
517	You're right to push. "Brave" can be a polite word for "the author didn't know how to end it." Let me make the case against.
518

520	
521	**It might be avoidance disguised as restraint.**
522	
523	Ending a novel is hard. One way to dodge the difficulty is to simply stop and call it ambiguity. The "blood on the snow" ending could read as the author refusing to commit—not trusting themselves to land the plane, so they bail out early and frame it as a choice.
524	
525	**Farrell's arc goes unresolved.**
526	
527	The novel has been building toward something in Farrell—recognition of his double, the peace he feels watching the buffalo, the journal that explains everything. Ending with him standing in an empty valley gives us no sense of what the journey did to him. He found the man. He read the confession. He witnessed the sacred thing depart. And then... nothing? Not even a physical response? He just stands there and the book ends?
528	
529	The current version—the peace, the collapse, even the fragments of rescue—at least shows Farrell changed by what he's witnessed. Cutting to "blood on the snow" removes all evidence of interiority at the moment when interiority matters most.
530	
531	**The climax already happened off-page.**
532	
533	Morrow's death is the dramatic peak, and we didn't see it. We arrived after. The white buffalo leaving is the aftermath of the aftermath. Ending there might feel not like resonance but like anticlimax—the book building toward a confrontation that never quite happens, then stopping before we can process what did.
534	
535	**"Blood on the snow" is a common image.**
536	
537	It's evocative, but it's also generic—the kind of image that appears in countless Westerns, war novels, frontier stories. Is it distinctive enough to carry the weight of this particular novel's ending? Or does it feel like reaching for a stock image because the specific one hasn't been found?
538	
539	**It might read as nihilistic rather than open.**
540	
541	The current ending offers something: the buffalo going home, Farrell's peace, the suggestion of survival. Cut all that and you're left with emptiness and blood. Full stop. That's a statement—but is it the statement this novel is making? The book has been about the *search* for meaning, not the absence of meaning. Morrow found what he was looking for. Farrell found something too, even if he can't name it. Ending on "blood on the snow" might flatten all of that into mere bleakness.
542	
543	**Readers might not know the novel is over.**
544	
545	Practical concern: without any signal of conclusion—no coda, no chapter after, no sense of winding down—readers may turn the page expecting more. The abruptness might create confusion before it creates resonance.
546	
547	**The current ending exists because something felt incomplete.**
548	
549	You wrote those additional sections. The collapse, the rescue, the Lakota perspective—you reached for them because the story felt unfinished without them. That instinct wasn't wrong. It was responding to a real gap. Cutting back might reopen the gap rather than reveal a cleaner shape underneath.
550	
551	---
552	
553	So the question is: does "blood on the snow" feel like the novel arriving at its true destination, or does it feel like the novel stopping short?

557	## USER
558	
559	Even if we won't necessarily want to show it, let's figure out if there's a viable scenario in which Farrell could survive his immediate circumstances and eventually make his way back to Aldridge. Giving him the benefit of the doubt on the delirium tremens aspect, though. Could he do so unaided? Is this only feasible if he is rescued? If so, who might rescue him and is this a realistic outcome?

562	
563	## ASSISTANT
564	
565	Let me think through the logistics.
566	
567	---
568	
569	## Farrell's condition at the moment he collapses
570	
571	**Physical state:**
572	- Deep alcohol withdrawal, but probably past the acute phase. DTs typically peak at 48-72 hours after last drink and resolve within 5-7 days. He's been without whiskey for well over a week. The seizures and worst hallucinations would be tapering. Still weak, malnourished, exhausted—but the immediate risk of withdrawal death (cardiac event, fatal seizure) is diminishing.
573	- Hypothermic or near-hypothermic. Lying in snow in a Nebraska winter, he has hours at most before death.
574	- Sweating from withdrawal makes wet clothing worse for heat retention.
575	
576	**Resources:**
577	- The horse is nearby, reins trailing. Horses often stay close to fallen riders.
578	- He has the journal, his rifle, presumably basic gear.
579	- No food, no whiskey.
580	
581	**Location:**
582	- A valley somewhere north of the Niobrara, deep in Lakota territory.
583	- The Hardins' homestead is several days' ride south.
584	- The trading post is further still—maybe a week in good conditions.
585	
586	---
587	
588	## Unaided survival: difficult but not impossible
589	
590	The scenario would require:
591	
592	1. **He wakes up before freezing.** This is the critical window—maybe two to three hours in those conditions, less if he's wet. If he's in a slight depression or the wind is blocked, maybe longer.
593	
594	2. **The horse is still there.** It is, in the current text. A horse standing nearby provides a psychological anchor and a means of travel. Some horses will nuzzle or stand over a fallen rider, which might rouse him.
595	
596	3. **He can get moving.** He's been established as extraordinarily stubborn—survived Mexico, survived a decade of slow drowning, tracked Morrow through withdrawal hallucinations. The novel has built him as someone who doesn't die easily.
597	
598	4. **He heads south by instinct.** He doesn't need to navigate precisely. South is warmer, south is the river, south is where he came from. If he can stay on the horse and keep moving, he might reach the Hardins' abandoned homestead (shelter, maybe remaining food stores) or even the trading post.
599	
600	5. **The weather cooperates minimally.** Not a blizzard, not the worst cold. Just winter.
601	
602	This is at the edge of plausibility, but not beyond it. It requires luck, but not miraculous luck.
603	
604	---
605	
606	## Rescue scenarios
607	
608	**The Lakota:**
609	
610	The current Chapter Twelve has Wears His Horses Out explicitly deciding *not* to help: "The white man's fate was his own." But this could be revised—he could reconsider, or a different group could find Farrell.
611	
612	*Problem:* This introduces a whole new narrative thread. Who are they? Why do they help? What happens during his recovery? It opens complications the novel would then need to address or deliberately leave unaddressed. It also risks feeling like a deus ex machina.
613	
614	*Possibility:* A more minimal version—they leave supplies, or they move his body somewhere sheltered, without nursing him back to health. A gesture rather than a rescue. But even this requires them to reverse the decision currently on the page.
615	
616	**Other travelers:**
617	
618	Trappers, traders, a mail carrier. Someone passing through.
619	
620	*Problem:* In deep winter, in that remote valley, the odds of someone appearing are low. This would feel like pure luck—possible, but not satisfying as an explanation.
621	
622	**Self-rescue to a waypoint:**
623	
624	The most plausible version might be: Farrell rouses himself (perhaps the horse nuzzles him, perhaps the cold itself shocks him awake), gets on the horse, and rides south on instinct. He makes it to the Hardins' homestead—where there's shelter, a stove, maybe cached food—and collapses again. He recovers there, alone, over days or weeks. Then continues to the trading post when he's able.
625	
626	This distributes the implausibility. He doesn't need one miraculous rescue; he needs to survive long enough to reach a place where survival is possible.
627	
628	---
629	
630	## Getting back to Aldridge
631	
632	Once he's at the trading post or a similar settlement, the journey east is hard but straightforward:
633	
634	- He has Morrow's journal as evidence.
635	- He knows the route—he came that way.
636	- He can wait for weather, recover strength, resupply.
637	- The trip is long but not unprecedented. People crossed this country routinely.
638	
639	The question is whether he *wants* to return. The novel suggests he feels an obligation—he kept following Morrow even after finding the graves, partly because the job felt unfinished. Delivering the journal and the truth to Aldridge would complete the commission.
640	
641	---

643	## For the novel's purposes
644	
645	You probably don't need to show any of this. What you need is for it to be *possible*—for a reader who thinks about it not to find an obvious impossibility.
646	
647	The current ending (the one we're considering cutting to "blood on the snow") is ambiguous about whether he survives. That ambiguity is sustainable if survival is plausible even though uncertain. I think it is: Farrell is resilient, the horse is there, the trading post is reachable, and the worst of the DTs are behind him.
648	
649	If you *do* want to imply survival without showing it, the fragments in the current Chapter Eleven ("a sensation of being lifted, of movement, of voices speaking in a language I did not understand") gesture toward Lakota rescue without committing to it. But you've already identified problems with that passage.
650	
651	The cleanest solution might be: trust that survival is possible, don't explain it, let the reader decide.
652

657	Establishing food and fuel caches at the Hardins seems like a Pareto fix here:
658	- shows that they would have been able to survive if not for Morrow
659	- shows that Morrow (or other parties) did not ransack the homestead
660	- these facts would also come up naturally during a thorough investigation by Farrell

663	
664	The presence of Farrell's horse might be given a bit more prominence given how crucial it is to his survival. Farrell would certainly be aware of this fact as much as anyone.
665	
666	This is all to say, let's see if we can make "blood on the snow" work honestly, where its ambiguity is not (just) an indication of bailing out.

27	Beyond her, at the far end of the valley, the herd stood bunched and dark. None of them came near.
28	
29	I had my rifle. I could have raised it, sighted on her, put a bullet through her heart. My hands shook, but at that distance, on an animal her size, they would have served. One shot, and the thing that had killed Josiah Morrow would be dead.
30	
31	I did not raise the rifle.
32	
33	She was not my enemy. She had done what her nature demanded.
34	
35	I sat back on my heels and looked at her. She looked back at me.
36	
37	---
38	
39	The visions came again, but they were different now.
40	
41	The soldiers were still there, standing in their silent circle, but they no longer seemed threatening. They were just men—dead men, men I had known, men I had fought beside and watched die. They had followed me all this way, and now they stood witness.
42	
43	Catherine Hardin was there too. She stood beside the body of the man who had killed her, her face composed, her hands folded in front of her. She did not look at me. She was watching the white buffalo without wonder.
44	
45	---
46	
47	Time passed. I do not know how much.
48	
49	The sun moved behind the clouds, invisible but present, its light changing from gray to paler gray to a thin yellow. The wind picked up, then died away. The white buffalo stood where she had stood, motionless, patient.
50	
51	And then she turned.
52	
53	She turned away from me, slowly, and began to walk north, toward the ridges that rose at the edge of the valley.
54	
55	I watched her go. Her white coat moved through the snow like a ship through water, and in the strange light of that winter morning she seemed to carry her own illumination.
56	
57	She was halfway across the meadow when I saw the others.
58	
59	They were on the ridge to the north, three or four of them. Men on horseback, dressed in furs and leather, dark against the snow. I had not seen them come. They sat their horses and watched as the white buffalo approached.
60	
61	Lakota, I thought. Or another vision—another gift from the fever.
62	
63	Behind me the horse shifted, his ears gone forward toward the ridge. He had never once taken notice of the soldiers.
64	
65	One of them looked toward me. The one in front—the leader, I judged. His eyes found me across the meadow, a figure kneeling in the snow beside a body, blood on the ground. He looked at me for a long moment. The others sat their horses and did not look at me at all. No sign passed, of welcome or of warning. Then he turned away.
66	
67	The white buffalo reached them. They turned their horses, and she fell in among them, and together they moved north, toward the ridges.
68	
69	I watched until they disappeared over the ridge.
70	
71	Behind me, the horse waited. I could hear him shifting in the snow, his breath coming in slow clouds. He would carry me south if I could reach him—back to the creek, back to the homestead where the Hardins had laid in enough supplies to last a winter, and her letters in their box, back to Oswego and the hundred dollars owed me on the answer in my saddlebag, back to the living world. He would carry me, if I could make myself move.
72	
73	I was not moving. I was kneeling in an empty valley beside a man I had never met, with blood on the snow and nothing left to follow.

content.content:
1	# Chapter One
2	
3	Ephraim Aldridge had not been inside a tavern in thirty years. He stood now in the doorway of this one, a low-ceilinged room thick with pipe smoke and the smell of men who worked outdoors, and he understood that he had been wrong to think thirty years sufficient preparation.
4	
5	The place was called The Broken Oar, though they were fifty miles from any water that would require one. It sat at the edge of the town, where the last of the frame houses gave way to forest. November had stripped the trees, and through the tavern's single window Aldridge could see the gray lattice of branches against a grayer sky.
6	
7	He removed his hat. Several men looked up from their drinks, weighed him, looked away. He was not what they expected to see, and they had already determined he was not their concern.
8	
9	The barman was a heavy-set man with a beard that had not been trimmed in some time. He watched Aldridge approach without expression.
10	
11	"I am looking for a man," Aldridge said.
12	
13	"We have several."
14	
15	"His name is Farrell. Henry Farrell."
16	
17	The barman's expression did not change, but something behind it did. "And who's looking?"
18	
19	Aldridge had prepared for this. In his business—shipping, dry goods, the movement of capital across the Great Lakes—preparation was everything. He had prepared for this journey as he prepared for all ventures. He had worn his second-best coat, the one that suggested prosperity without ostentation. He had left his pocket watch in his room at the boarding house. He had rehearsed what he would say.
20	
21	None of it seemed adequate now.
22	
23	"My name is Ephraim Aldridge. I have come from Oswego. I have a matter that requires a man of particular capabilities, and I have been told that Farrell possesses them."
24	
25	"Told by who?"
26	
27	"A man named Garrett, at the lumber office."
28	
29	The barman considered this. Then he turned and spoke to someone Aldridge could not see, in a back room. There was a murmured exchange. The barman turned back.
30	
31	"He's not here."
32	
33	"I was told he would be."
34	
35	"He was. He left an hour ago."
36	
37	Aldridge felt something tighten in his chest. He had been traveling for four days. The first day by railroad to Syracuse and Rome, then the cars north to Watertown, then a coach east into country that grew steadily wilder and less familiar. He had not expected the search itself to be easy, but he had expected that when he found the man, the man would be there to be found.
38	
39	"Where did he go?"
40	
41	The barman shrugged. "Didn't say."
42	
43	"When will he return?"
44	
45	"Didn't say that either."
46	
47	Aldridge stood in the smoke and the noise and felt the accumulated exhaustion of the journey settle into him. He was fifty-eight years old. His daughter was dead or in danger, and he was standing in a tavern in a town he had never heard of six months ago, asking after a man who had already left.
48	
49	"I'll wait," he said.
50	
51	The barman's expression flickered. "As you like. Drink?"
52	
53	"No. Thank you."
54	
55	The barman shrugged and turned away.
56	
57	Aldridge found a table near the window. He sat with his back to the wall, his hat on the table in front of him. The hat was beaver felt, well-made, incongruous. He left it there anyway.
58	
59	The afternoon passed. Men came and went. Some of them glanced at Aldridge; most did not. He watched the gray light fade toward evening, watched the barman light candles and then lamps. His thoughts moved in circles that had become familiar over the past months: Catherine's last letter, dated July. The silence since. The things a man might do to a woman, alone on the frontier, far from anyone who might help her.
60	
61	He had not approved of the marriage. George Hardin was a farmer's son from Ohio, a man with more ambition than sense, who had filled Catherine's head with talk of land and opportunity and the future that awaited them in the West. Aldridge had argued against it. He had threatened to cut her off. In the end he had withdrawn both, because she was his only child and her mother was dead and he could not bear to lose her entirely.
62	
63	So he had let her go. Nearly three years now, and no grandchildren. He had expected—hoped, at least—that a child might bring her back East, or bring him West to meet it. Her letters had said nothing on the subject, which he took as its own kind of answer. Another sign that the marriage was not what it should be. Another reason to worry.
64	
65	And now she was gone.
66	
67	The door opened, letting in a gust of cold air. A man entered, and Aldridge knew at once that this was Farrell.
68	
69	He was not what Aldridge had expected. The men at the lumber office had spoken of him in terms that suggested something dangerous, something barely contained. But the man who stood in the doorway, stamping snow from his boots, looked merely tired. He was of medium height, lean, with a face that had been weathered past his years. His coat was worn but adequate. He carried no visible weapon, though Aldridge supposed a man like this would not need to make such things visible.
70	
71	Farrell's eyes went around the room once. They stopped on Aldridge for a moment—the only man sitting alone, the only man who did not belong—and then moved on. He walked to the bar.
72	
73	The barman spoke to him, low. Farrell listened. Then he turned and looked at Aldridge again, this time with something more than casual interest.
74	
75	He crossed the room and stood at Aldridge's table. Up close, his eyes were pale, the color difficult to determine in the lamplight. He did not sit.
76	
77	"You've been waiting," he said.
78	
79	"Yes."
80	
81	"Garrett sent you."
82	
83	"He directed me. He did not send me. I came of my own accord."
84	
85	Farrell considered this distinction. "Why?"
86	
87	"I have a proposition. May I buy you a drink?"
88	
89	"No." But he pulled out a chair and sat, folding his hands on the table. His hands were calloused, the knuckles scarred. "Say what you came to say, Mr. Aldridge."
90	
91	Aldridge had rehearsed this too. He had written it out, back in Oswego, before he left. He had refined it during the journey, honing each phrase until it conveyed precisely what he needed to convey and nothing more. Now the words seemed foolish.
92	
93	"My daughter," he said. "Her name is Catherine. She married a man named George Hardin nearly three years ago, against my wishes. They went west. Nebraska Territory, or thereabouts. She wrote to me regularly—every month, sometimes more often. This past year they came a little slower, but they came. They stopped in July."
94	
95	Farrell's expression did not change. He was listening, but not reacting. Aldridge found this more unnerving than hostility would have been.
96	
97	"I have made inquiries," Aldridge continued. "I have written to every authority I could identify—federal, territorial, military. The responses have been unhelpful. The territory is vast, and there are many homesteads, and records are not kept as they would be in the East. No one knows anything about the Hardins. No one has seen them. No one can tell me if my daughter is alive or dead."
98	
99	"And you want me to find out."
100	
101	"Yes."
102	
103	"Why me?"
104	
105	Aldridge had expected this question. "Because the men at the lumber office, and the men I spoke to before them, say that you have done this kind of work before. Finding people. Learning things. And because—" He hesitated.
106	
107	"And because they say I'm not particular about what happens when I find them."
108	
109	Aldridge said nothing.
110	
111	Farrell leaned back in his chair. "What do you think happened to your daughter, Mr. Aldridge?"
112	
113	"I think her husband killed her."
114	
115	Aldridge had not said the words aloud before. He had thought them, in the small hours of the night when sleep would not come. He had written them in a letter he did not send. But he had not spoken them until now.
116	
117	"Why?"
118	
119	"Because the letters stopped. Because she would have written to me, if she could. Because I know—" He stopped, collected himself. "Because I know that she was unhappy. Her last letters were not like the others. She did not say so directly, but I could tell. A father knows."
120	
121	Farrell watched him for a long moment. Then he said: "You want me to find your daughter. And if she's dead, you want me to deal with her husband."
122	
123	"Yes."
124	
125	"Deal with him how?"
126	
127	"As you judge necessary."
128	
129	The silence stretched. Someone laughed at the bar. Aldridge waited.
130	
131	"The territory is large," Farrell said. "Winter is coming. Travel will be difficult."
132	
133	"I understand."
134	
135	"I may not find her. I may not find anything."
136	
137	"I understand that too."
138	
139	"And if I do find her—if she's alive, and simply stopped writing—what then?"
140	
141	Aldridge had not prepared for this question. He found he did not have an answer.
142	
143	"Then you tell me," he said finally. "And I will decide what to do."
144	
145	Farrell nodded slowly. He seemed to be calculating something. "It will cost you."
146	
147	"I expected as much."
148	
149	"Two hundred dollars. Half now, half when I return with an answer. Expenses on top of that."
150	
151	It was a large sum. Not ruinous, for a man of Aldridge's means, but large. He did not hesitate.
152	
153	"Agreed."
154	
155	He reached into his coat and withdrew an envelope. He had prepared this too, back in Oswego. The bills were crisp, counted three times. He slid the envelope across the table.
156	
157	Farrell took it, glanced inside, did not count. He folded the envelope and put it in his own coat.
158	
159	"I'll need to know everything you know. Her letters, if you have them. The location of the homestead, as best you can determine. The husband's name and history, anything that might be useful."
160	
161	"I have prepared a packet. It is at my room, at the boarding house."
162	
163	"I'll come by in the morning."
164	
165	Farrell stood. He looked down at Aldridge.
166	
167	"You should prepare yourself, Mr. Aldridge. For what I might find."
168	
169	"I have prepared myself."
170	
171	"No," Farrell said. "You haven't."
172	
173	He turned and walked to the bar, spoke briefly with the barman, and then was gone, out into the night. The door closed behind him, and the cold air that had followed him in was absorbed into the warmth of the room.
174	
175	Aldridge sat at his table for a long time, the beaver-felt hat before him. The letters were back at the boarding house, waiting for the man who would carry them west. He did not need to look at them again. He had read them so many times that he knew them by heart. The early ones, full of hope and descriptions of the land. The middle ones, more measured, the hope beginning to curdle. And the last one, dated the twentieth of July, in which she had hoped the worst was behind them.
176	
177	He had not known, when he read it, that it would be the last.
178	
179	The barman came by, asked again if he wanted a drink. This time Aldridge said yes. He drank it without tasting it, paid, and left. The night was cold, colder than it had been when he arrived, and the walk back to the boarding house was long. But he walked it.
180	
181	In the morning, Farrell came for the packet. He untied it at the table, counted the letters, and held the daguerreotype to the window light for a long moment before putting it away. Aldridge gave him the map he had drawn from memory and hope, and a description of George Hardin that relied too much on his own animosity to be trusted. Farrell took it all without comment.
182	
183	"How long?" Aldridge asked.
184	
185	"Months. Maybe longer. Depends on what I find, and where."
186	
187	"And you'll send word?"
188	
189	"If I can."
190	
191	They shook hands. Farrell's grip was firm, businesslike. Then he was gone, walking west along the main street, and Aldridge stood in the doorway of the boarding house and watched him until he disappeared around a corner.
192	
193	He had done what he could. He had sent a man to find his daughter, to learn the truth, to deliver justice if justice was warranted. It was out of his hands now.
194	
195	He went back inside, packed his bag, and began the long journey home. The country outside the coach window was bleak and cold, the fields fallow, the trees bare. He watched it pass and thought of Catherine, and of the man he had hired to find her, and of what that man might do when he did.
196	
197	He did not want to think about that last part too closely. He found that this was why he had hired Farrell in the first place—so that he would not have to.
198	
199	The coach rattled on, east toward Oswego.
